Clocks, more than the sun, set the hours at which people work and sleep \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. Daylight saving time (DST) relies on this to move an hour of light from the morning to the evening. Whether to keep moving the clock is an open question in many countries. In the United States, the Senate passed a bill making DST permanent in 2022 and the House of Representatives passed another in 2026, which awaits the Senate \citep{uscongress2022sunshine, uscongress2026sunshine}; the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end seasonal clock changes and leave each member state to choose a permanent time, a proposal still awaiting the Council \citep{europarl2019seasonal}; Mexico abolished DST in 2022 \citep{mexico2022ley}. Brazil, which had moved its clocks every summer since 1985, abolished DST in April 2019 \citep{brasil2019decreto}. Since then, from November to February, the sun has set an hour earlier on the clock in the states where 131 million Brazilians live \citep{ibge2023censo}. The national grid operator has since studied bringing it back \citep{ons2024nota}. The stakes on the road are potentially large: crashes killed 37,150 people in Brazil in 2024, 15 percent of them pedestrians \citep{datasus2025sim}, and road traffic kills about 1.19 million people a year worldwide \citep{who2023global}. % national_road_deaths.rds (13_design_descriptives.R): 2024, 37,150 deaths, 15.3 percent pedestrians.

The choice between permanent regimes matters because daily schedules are coordinated: work and leisure are worth more when they coincide with other people's \citep{hamermesh2008cues}. A clock rule therefore moves the whole society's day relative to daylight at once. Two forces then set its cost on the road. People reduce their exposure to hazards they know about, so the harm one observes is net of that avoidance \citep{neidell2009information}; on the road, the avoidance is travel that moves out of the dark. Schedules respond to the clock as well: under DST, people appear to move some activities earlier in the day \citep{sexton2014behavioral}. And drivers do not bear the full risk their driving imposes on others \citep{edlin2006accident}, pedestrians and cyclists among them \citep{crandall1984automobile, white2004arms}. Avoidance limits the deaths a darker evening adds, and the externality leaves drivers avoiding less than the risk to others would warrant. Neither argument says how many deaths remain once travel has adjusted, or whether a brighter morning gives them back. The evidence on DST and road safety comes mostly from the clock changes themselves, comparing crashes in the days or weeks just before the clocks move with those just after \citep{sullivan2002role, sood2007short, smith2016spring, laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight}. A clock change shifts daylight relative to clock time overnight. Because work and school schedules remain largely unchanged, comparisons around the transition capture the effect of light before travel patterns have had time to adjust. Each change also adds a second shock, a night with an hour less or more of sleep. A change of regime observed over several seasons has neither limitation: it involves no lost night, and travel has time to adjust.

This paper uses Brazil's abolition to estimate how many deaths remain once travel has adjusted and whether the brighter morning gives them back. Because DST advanced the clock by exactly one hour, each municipality has, on each summer day, one clock hour in the evening that went from daylight to darkness. It is the hour after sunset in standard time, which was the last hour of sunlight under DST and has been the first hour after sunset since abolition. We compute that hour from the solar position at each municipal seat on each date, and do the same for the hour after standard-time sunrise, which went the other way, from darkness to daylight. A triple difference then compares events in the hour that turned dark in the 11 states that had DST in every southern-hemisphere summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 with the same hour in 12 states that had none in those summers, in the summer window against the months from April to August, before and after abolition. Because the affected hour follows local sunset across municipalities and dates, a confounding regional trend would need to align with this shifting hour to explain the estimate. The hours immediately before and after experienced smaller changes in ambient light, from full sun to low sun or from twilight to night, and therefore provide a further check on whether the response follows the change in light. A second design uses every clock hour of the day, each weighted by how much abolition changed its light, computed from the position of the sun. With a separate effect for each clock hour on each date, it tests whether the deaths follow the sun or the clock, and it counts the net change over the day without choosing hours.

Two independent high-quality registers measure the outcome. Death certificates, from the Ministry of Health's Mortality Information System (SIM), record the clock time of death, which is close to the time of the crash for those who die on the road, and cover every public road in the country. The publicly available crash records of the Federal Highway Police (PRF) cover every crash its officers attend on federal highways, together with the light conditions the officer saw. The officers' records show that the evening hour did turn dark: after abolition, the share of crashes in that hour that officers recorded at dusk or night rose by 24 percentage points.

After abolition, road deaths in the hour that turned dark rose by 29.2 log points (34 percent), from an average of 110 per summer in the 11 treated states. Deaths and injury crashes on federal highways rose by 54 and 22 log points (71 and 25 percent). All three estimates remain significant under three forms of inference that do not rely on asymptotics with 23 clusters: a score wild bootstrap of the Poisson model, a wild cluster bootstrap of its linear analogue and a permutation of the treated states. The effect follows the local sun rather than the clock. With a separate effect for every clock hour on every date, a clock hour that goes from full daylight to night has 48 log points more road deaths, and the estimate holds when it rests only on how the time of sunset differs across the treated states and the dates of the summer.

For road deaths, the season-by-season estimates before abolition show no differential trend. Without the pandemic months the estimate is 23 log points; in the summer window alone, without the off-season comparison, it is 34 and stable across the five seasons without DST. It keeps its size, though not its precision, under an imputation estimator that extrapolates a pre-abolition trend, and it holds when any single state or season is left out. On federal highways, injury crashes show a trend before abolition, and both federal highway estimates shrink once a trend is allowed. The size of the effect therefore comes from road deaths. The federal highway records serve two other purposes: they show that the hour did turn dark, and they inform the mechanism, either on the seasons in which crashes show no trend (crashes per vehicle) or with the pre-abolition trend extrapolated (the split by road user). The rise is concentrated in the hour that turned dark and the next one, which went from twilight to night. Road deaths at midday and at night, whose light did not change and where an effect of sleep would also appear, do not rise.

Pedestrians bear a disproportionate share of the increase. They were 12 percent of road deaths in the hour that turned dark before abolition and account for 43 percent of the excess after it. Their deaths in that hour more than doubled, a rise of 77 log points (115 percent), against 18 log points (20 percent) for all other road users. Travel responded to light as well. Hourly counts at the federal highway stations of the National Traffic Count Plan show that traffic in the hour that turned dark fell by about 6 percent and traffic in the morning hour that turned light rose by about 12 percent. Under permutation inference, the first change is borderline and the second is not significant. Over the summers covered by the traffic counts, the risk of an injury crash per vehicle in the hour that turned dark rose by 24 log points (27 percent), more than crashes themselves.

The morning does not give the deaths back. Road deaths in the hour after sunrise, which turned light, show no detectable change ($-3$ log points, standard error 12). Weighting every hour of the day by how much its light changed, and assuming that hours that remained in full daylight or full darkness were unaffected, abolition added 62 road deaths per summer window, from 15 November to 14 February (standard error 12). This is the count most directly supported by the observed summer window. Extending the estimate to the full DST season gives 74 deaths (standard error 14). These counts include only deaths at the scene with a recorded time; scaling them to deaths without a recorded time and to deaths off the road, most of them in hospitals, raises the summer-window count to between 77 and 157. Estimated over the whole day without assuming which hours were affected, the change is too imprecise (standard error 66) to confirm the count or rule it out. At a value of a statistical life transferred to Brazil's income \citep{robinson2019valuing}, the deaths in one summer window have an estimated cost of 114 million 2025 international dollars (a unit with the purchasing power that a US dollar has in the United States), rising to 287 million under the broadest scaling. On the other side of the ledger, the Ministry of Mines and Energy had concluded before abolition that DST no longer saved electricity, possibly because patterns of electricity consumption had changed, particularly through increased late-night air-conditioning demand \citep{mme2019nota}.

The clock changes before 2019 show the same change of light before travel had time to adjust: for three weeks after each change, the evening hour was dark (after February) or light (after October) while travel kept to the same clock hours. Read as the effect of a darker evening, the changes give 42 log points (standard error 14), against 29 after abolition. The estimate over the whole window, however, averages weeks in which the effect differs. Abolition raised road deaths in hour 0 by 58 log points (13) from mid-November to early December and by 49 (16) in the second half of January, but left no detectable change from Christmas to mid-January (24 December to 15 January). The weeks after the clock changes fall while schools are in session, as do the weeks from mid-November to early December, and in those weeks the effect of abolition is statistically indistinguishable from the effect at the clock changes. This holds both when hour 0 is compared across states and when it is compared with other hours of the same day, a specification that absorbs shocks common to all hours of a day, including the sleep effects of the clock changes. Five summers after abolition, we find no sign that the effect of a darker evening had faded as travel adjusted, although the comparison cannot rule out a moderate decline.

The paper contributes to three literatures. The first estimates the effect of DST on road safety, mostly from the clock changes: in the United States \citep{sood2007short, smith2016spring}, Greece \citep{laliotis2023summertime}, Chile \citep{gillmore2025daylight}, Brazil \citep{franco2023daylight} and Mexico \citep{goodwin2024impact}. These studies attribute the deaths that follow the spring change to lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, and find that the light DST adds to the evening lowers serious crashes \citep{laliotis2023summertime, gillmore2025daylight} or mainly moves deaths between hours of the day \citep{smith2016spring}. Even \citet{depalo2023should}, who explicitly asks whether DST should be abolished, relies on clock transitions to answer that question. Closest to the question of regimes, \citet{bunnings2021spring} estimate the effect of darkness on crashes in Great Britain from the variation in sunrise and sunset times across places and dates, and simulate that year-round DST would save 8 percent of the cost of darkness. \citet{coate2004effects} estimate that year-round DST would avoid 171 pedestrian deaths a year in the United States, and \citet{ferguson1995daylight} that it would have avoided about 900 fatal crashes in 1987--1991, four fifths of them involving pedestrians. This paper observes a change of regime rather than simulating one, over five seasons and with a first stage recorded by third parties, and compares it with the same change of light at the clock changes, before travel adjusted. It also locates the deaths in the evening hour and among pedestrians, the road users whose crash risk is most sensitive to ambient light \citep{sullivan2002role, woods2025daylight}, even to the brightness of the moon \citep{tyndall2025road}.

The second literature uses DST to identify the effect of ambient light on behavior, mostly crime \citep{doleac2015under, tealde2022unequal, dominguez2023crime}; in Brazil, homicides by firearm fell during the months of DST, mostly in the early-evening hours that DST lit \citep{toro2016daylight}. These studies, like this one, look for the effect in the hours whose light the clock moves. Here the shift of light is permanent, and it arrives without the change in sleep that a clock change brings.

The third literature weighs the costs and benefits of DST. It has measured mostly energy use \citep{kellogg2008daylight, kotchen2011does} and, through sleep, health and productivity \citep{gibson2018time, giuntella2019sunset}. The road-safety studies above measure mostly the transitions, which a choice between permanent regimes removes either way. This paper adds the road deaths of the regime itself.

Relative to these literatures, the paper makes three contributions. First, it estimates the road-safety consequences of an actual change in clock regime, observed over five summers, rather than inferring them from short windows around clock transitions or from simulations. Second, because the hour that turned dark is set by the local sun, the design separates the effect of light from the effects of the clock and of sleep, and it shows that the light gained in the morning does not offset the light lost in the evening. Third, it values the additional road deaths and compares their cost with the energy estimates at the center of Brazil's DST policy debate.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} describes Brazil's DST and its abolition, Section~\ref{sec:data} the data and Section~\ref{sec:design} the design. Section~\ref{sec:results} reports the results and Section~\ref{sec:cost} their cost. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Daylight Saving Time in Brazil and Its Abolition}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{The policy}

Brazil observed DST every summer from 1985/86 to 2018/19. The states covered changed often in the 1990s; from 2008 a standing decree fixed both the dates and the states \citep{brasil2008decreto}. Clocks moved forward at midnight on the third Sunday of October (from 2018, the first Sunday of November; \citealp{brasil2017decreto}) and back on the third Sunday of February, a week later when that Sunday fell on Carnival. DST applied in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paran\'a, S\~ao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Esp\'irito Santo, Minas Gerais, Goi\'as, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and the Federal District, which held 131 million of Brazil's 203 million people in 2022 \citep{ibge2023censo}. Within the sample, Bahia had DST only in 2011/12 and Tocantins only in 2012/13. The North and the rest of the Northeast, close to the equator, where the length of the day varies little over the year, did not have DST in this period. Figure~\ref{fig:map} maps the groups.

Decree 9,772 of 25 April 2019 abolished DST in the whole country \citep{brasil2019decreto}. It followed a technical note of the Ministry of Mines and Energy that concluded that DST had stopped delivering the electricity savings it was designed for \citep{mme2019nota}. By the ministry's estimate, the 2018/19 season had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent: savings on evening lighting were outweighed by higher consumption late at night, which the note attributed tentatively to air-conditioning. The debate did not end there. In 2024 the national grid operator estimated that reinstating DST would lower the evening peak, which rooftop solar generation has made the binding constraint on the system, and save 96 to 139 million international dollars (R\$244 to 356 million) in thermal-generation fuel in one summer \citep{ons2024nota}.

\subsection{What abolition changed}

DST adds no light to the day; it moves the clock. Panel A of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows the clock time of sunset and sunrise in S\~ao Paulo over 2018/19, under the DST then in force and without it. In mid-January the sun set at 7:58 p.m.\ on the clock under DST and now sets at 6:58 p.m.; it rose at 6:32 a.m.\ and now rises at 5:32 a.m. % São Paulo, 15 January, NOAA equations (EXPLICANDO_O_PROJETO.md, section 1.2).
Because work, school and the commute keep to the clock, abolition put the people who used to travel in the last hour of sunlight on the road after sunset.

Let $s_{md}$ be the clock time of sunset in standard time at municipality $m$ on day $d$. Under DST the clock ran an hour ahead, so the sun set at clock time $s_{md}+60$ minutes and was above the horizon throughout the clock hour $[s_{md}, s_{md}+60)$. Since abolition the sun has been below the horizon throughout that hour. We call it hour 0, or the hour that turned dark. Its morning counterpart, the clock hour $[r_{md}, r_{md}+60)$ after standard-time sunrise $r_{md}$, was dark under DST and is light now. The neighboring hours changed less: the hour before $s_{md}$ went from full sun to low sun, and the hour after $s_{md}+60$ from twilight to night.

\section{Data}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Deaths on the road}

The Mortality Information System (Sistema de Informa\c{c}\~oes sobre Mortalidade, SIM) of the Ministry of Health holds every death certificate issued in Brazil, with the underlying cause of death coded in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10), the municipality and type of place of occurrence, and the date and clock time of death \citep{datasus2025sim}. We select deaths from land-transport crashes (codes V01--V89) that occurred on a public road and call them road deaths. For a person who dies at the scene, the time of death is close to the time of the crash: when a federal highway crash with one death and a single road-death certificate fall in the same municipality and day, the certificate's time lies within the hour after the crash in 59 percent of the pairs, against 5 percent for pairs formed a week apart (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement}). For a person who dies in a hospital, it may be hours or days later. In-hospital deaths therefore never enter an hourly count. Between 15 and 20 percent of road deaths, depending on the group of states, the time of year and the period, have no clock time and drop out of every count as well. % pretrends.rds, missing_hour: 15.4 to 20.1 percent by group, window and period.
In the treated states, an average summer window before abolition had 2,382 road deaths with a clock time, 110 of them in hour 0 (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

The death register is the standard source on mortality in Brazil, including in economics \citep[for example,][who measure homicide with it]{dixcarneiro2018economic}. Its coverage rests on a legal requirement: no burial may take place without a death record, which the registry office issues on the basis of a physician's death certificate where a physician is available \citep[art.~77]{brasil1973lei}. DST abolition did not change how deaths are recorded. In a triple difference like that of Section~\ref{sec:design}, neither the share of land-transport deaths that occur on the road (half of them) nor the share of road deaths without a clock time moves with abolition (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:records} and Table~\ref{tab:measurement}).

\subsection{Crashes on federal highways}

The Federal Highway Police (Pol\'icia Rodovi\'aria Federal, PRF) publishes every crash its officers attend on federal highways, from 2007 to 2025, with date, clock time, municipality, numbers of people killed and injured, type of crash and the light conditions the officer observed: full daylight, dawn, dusk or night \citep{prf2025dados}. We use two outcomes. Federal highway deaths count people killed at the scene of the crash \citep{prf2025anuario}, the same concept as road deaths in the SIM. Federal highway injury crashes are crashes with at least one casualty, a person killed or injured. Crashes without casualties are not used: an online self-report gradually replaced police attendance for them, at different dates in different states, which breaks that series differently in the two groups. The two registers overlap only in part. Road deaths cover every public road, urban streets included; federal highways are intercity roads, mostly outside cities, where the treated states had 1,176 deaths per summer before abolition, against 2,382 road deaths (Table~\ref{tab:descriptives}).

\subsection{Traffic counts}\label{sec:counts}

The National Traffic Count Plan (Plano Nacional de Contagem de Tr\'afego, PNCT) of the federal roads agency (DNIT) publishes hourly vehicle counts, by direction and vehicle class, at continuous counting stations on federal highways \citep{dnit2025pnct}. We use complete station-days counted from 2014 to May 2019 and from May 2021 to 2025, which cover the summers 2014/15 to 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25.\footnote{DNIT's contract for continuous counts ended in June 2019. The values published for the second half of 2019 were estimated with a statistical model, and there were no counts in 2020 \citep[p.~7]{dnit2020nota}. A new contract was tendered in 2020 \citep{dnit2020edital} and signed on 30 December 2020 and 13 January 2021; counting resumed in May 2021. We drop every station-day from June 2019 to December 2020, and any station-day whose daily total repeats exactly on the same weekday one to four weeks apart, which marks a modeled value.}

\subsection{Sun and clock}

For each municipal seat and day we compute sunrise and sunset in standard time from the solar position equations of \citet{noaa2025solar}, using the seat coordinates from IBGE and the standard offset of the municipality's legal time zone \citep{brasil1913decreto, brasil2008lei, brasil2013lei}. Every death and crash is then placed in a 60-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset or sunrise at its municipality on its date. Using NOAA's full solar algorithm \citep{meeus1998astronomical} instead moves sunset by at most 1.6 minutes and the main estimate from 29.2 to 29.8 log points (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement}). The death certificates, the federal highway police records and the traffic counts all give legal clock time, the time on the clock under whatever regime was in force. Section~\ref{sec:firststage} shows this in the officers' records, and Online Appendix~\ref{app:data} in the death certificates and the traffic counts.

\subsection{Sample}

The treated group consists of the 10 states that had DST every summer from 2008/09 to 2018/19 and the Federal District, which contains the capital, Bras\'ilia, and has the powers of a state. We refer to these 11 units as the treated states. The control group is the 12 states of the North and Northeast without DST in the sample: Rond\^onia, Roraima, Par\'a, Amap\'a, Maranh\~ao, Piau\'i, Cear\'a, Rio Grande do Norte, Para\'iba, Pernambuco, Alagoas and Sergipe. We exclude Bahia and Tocantins, which had DST in one summer each, and Acre and Amazonas, which changed time zone during the sample (Figure~\ref{fig:map}). A season runs from July to June, so that each summer falls within one season, and is named by its first year. The sample runs from 2008/09, the first season under the 2008 decree, to 2023/24, the last for which the death register is final, so it has 11 seasons with DST and 5 without.

The summer window runs from 15 November to 14 February. Every day in it was under DST in every season before abolition: the latest start of DST in the sample was 4 November 2018 and the earliest end 15 February 2009. The same window is used in every season, before and after abolition, so no day in it is partly treated and the year-to-year variation in DST dates does not enter the comparison. The window starts at least 11 days after the latest start of DST and ends before the earliest end, so the weeks after clock changes, when the literature finds the effects of lost sleep \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight}, fall outside it. The off-season runs from 1 April to 31 August, when no state ever had DST. The estimation panel has one row per state and day in these two windows: 23 states and 245 days in each of 16 seasons, or 90,160 state-days.

In the treated states, road deaths in hour 0 rose from 110 to 141 per summer after abolition, while those in the same hour of the off-season fell from 362 to 313; in the control states both fell. Pedestrian deaths in hour 0 of the treated states' summer doubled, from 13 to 27 per summer, while they fell in the off-season and in the control states.

\section{Empirical Strategy}\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Specification}

For each state $s$ and day $d$ in the summer window or the off-season, let $y_{sd}$ count the events that occur in one hour bin, hour 0 unless stated otherwise. The main specification is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main}
  y_{sd} = \exp\big(\beta\, T_s W_d A_d + \alpha_{s,w(d)} + \gamma_{s,t(d)} + \delta_d\big)\,\varepsilon_{sd},
\end{equation}
where $T_s$ marks the 11 treated states, $W_d$ days in the summer window and $A_d$ seasons after abolition. The fixed effects are state by window ($\alpha$; summer window or off-season), state by season ($\gamma$) and date ($\delta$). We report $100\beta$, the effect in log points.

Each set of fixed effects removes a class of threats. State-by-window effects absorb every permanent difference between a state's summer and its off-season: tourism, the rainy season, and the fact that hour 0 falls at a later clock time in summer than in winter. State-by-season effects absorb anything that moves a state's counts proportionally in both windows of a season, such as its vehicle fleet, enforcement or the pandemic. Date effects absorb national holidays and national shocks. The coefficient $\beta$ is then identified by the change, after abolition, in the gap between the summer and the off-season of the treated states, relative to the same change in the control states. The identifying assumption is that, without abolition, that gap would have moved in parallel in the two groups.

We estimate equation~(\ref{eq:main}) by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, which requires only that the conditional mean be correct and handles the many zeros of a single hour's count \citep{santossilva2006log}: 88 percent of state-days have no road death in hour 0. The share of zeros implied by the fitted means matches the observed share within 1.1 percentage points in every outcome, and the ratio of the residual variance to the mean is between 0.9 and 1.6, so neither a zero-inflated nor a negative binomial model is needed. % inference.rds: zeros_obs_pct against zeros_poisson_pct, largest gap 1.05 (federal highway deaths, morning); dispersion 0.93 to 1.57.

The outcome is a single hour because, within the summer window alone, standard-time sunset differs across the municipalities of the sample by about two hours, so a fixed block of clock hours mixes hour 0 with hours whose light did not change and dilutes the effect. Hour 0 also predicts where an effect of light must appear and where it must not. A shock to the treated states' summers unrelated to light, such as a change in policing, has no reason to concentrate in the hour that follows standard-time sunset at each municipality on each date and to leave the hours on either side of it unaffected.

\subsection{Light or the clock: a dose of darkness}\label{sec:dose}

Hour 0 isolates light only if nothing else changed after 2019 at the clock time at which it falls. In the treated states' summer it falls later on the clock than in their off-season (in S\~ao Paulo, about 7 p.m.\ in January against 5:30 p.m.\ in June) and later than in the control states, closer to the equator. A change after 2019 in the risk at that time of the evening, anywhere in the country, would therefore bias $\beta$. A second design separates light from clock time. For each municipal seat, date and clock hour $h$, we compute from the solar position how dark the hour is without DST and how dark it was with it, counting a minute of night as 1, a minute of civil twilight (the sun less than six degrees below the horizon) as one half and a minute of daylight as 0. The difference is the change in darkness abolition brought to that clock hour. It runs from 1, for an evening hour that went from full daylight to night, to $-1$, for a morning hour that went the other way, and it sums to zero over each day, because abolition moved light rather than removing it. Averaged over each state's municipal seats, weighted by their road deaths before abolition, it gives $D_{sdh}$, and the model is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dose}
  y_{sdh} = \exp\big(\theta_e\, X_{sdh}\, \mathbf{1}[h \ge 12] + \theta_m\, X_{sdh}\, \mathbf{1}[h < 12] + \alpha_{s,h,w(d)} + \gamma_{s,h,t(d)} + \delta_{h,d}\big)\,\varepsilon_{sdh},
\end{equation}
where $X_{sdh} = T_s W_d A_d D_{sdh}$, on a panel of states, days and the 24 clock hours. Clock hours $h = 0, \dots, 23$ are split at noon into morning ($h < 12$) and evening ($h \ge 12$). The dose is non-zero only from 4 to 8 a.m.\ and from 5 to 10 p.m., so any cut between 8 a.m.\ and 5 p.m.\ gives the same split. Separate coefficients let the evening hours that turned dark and the morning hours that turned light have effects of different size, rather than forcing them to offset. % 23_light_dose.R dose: non-zero only at h = 4-7 (all negative) and h = 17-21 (all positive).
The clock-hour-by-date effects $\delta_{h,d}$ absorb any change in the risk at a given clock time on a given date anywhere in the country, so a change at particular times of the evening common to the whole country cannot drive $\theta_e$; Section~\ref{sec:dose-results} also removes changes specific to the treated states' clock hours. $\theta_e$ is the effect, in log points, of an evening clock hour going from full daylight to night, and $\theta_m$ that of a morning hour. Because every hour enters, with a dose of zero where the hour remained in full daylight or full darkness, the model also yields the net change in deaths over the day without choosing hours.

\subsection{Inference}

Standard errors are clustered by state. With 23 clusters, 11 of them treated, cluster-robust inference can over-reject \citep{cameron2008bootstrap}, so we report three further p-values. The first is from a score wild bootstrap of the Poisson model itself \citep{kline2012score}: the model is fitted with the null imposed, each state's score for the treatment term is multiplied by a random Webb weight, and the studentized score is compared with its distribution over 9,999 draws. The second is from a wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed, Webb weights and 9,999 draws \citep{webb2023reworking}, applied to the linear analogue of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) estimated by least squares on counts. The third is from permutation inference. In each of 999 draws, we assign the treatment to 11 of the 23 states at random and re-estimate the Poisson model. The p-value is the share of draws, counting the actual assignment, whose t-statistic is at least as large in absolute value as the actual one. The test compares t-statistics rather than estimates because states differ widely in size, and with heterogeneous clusters a test on the estimate can be unreliable while one on the t-statistic typically does better \citep{mackinnon2020randomization}. DST was not assigned at random, so the test asks whether an arbitrary group of 11 states would produce a t-statistic as large as that of the treated states.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The hour turned dark}\label{sec:firststage}

Panel B of Figure~\ref{fig:light} shows that hour 0 turned dark in the officers' records, and that the records use legal clock time. For crashes in the treated states' summer window, it plots the share recorded at dusk or night by 10-minute bin of clock time relative to standard-time sunset. Under DST, that share reached one half at standard-time sunset; without DST, it reaches one half 50 minutes earlier. The curve moved by close to the hour the clock moved, which is what legal clock time implies. In hour 0 of the treated states, officers recorded 74 percent of crashes at dusk or night before abolition, and a linear version of the triple difference of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) gives a rise of 23.6 percentage points (standard error 2.0) in that share. % light_dose.rds, first_stage: fs_pp, fs_se_pp, treated_pre_dark_pct.
The record is a coarse measure of light. Officers recorded many crashes in the last hour of sunlight as dusk, so the 24 points understate the change from sun above the horizon to sun below it. The dose of Section~\ref{sec:dose} measures darkness from the sun instead.

Panel A of Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the main estimates. In the hour that turned dark, road deaths rose by 29.2 log points (standard error 9.0), or 34 percent. Federal highway deaths rose by 53.9 log points (20.3) and federal highway injury crashes by 22.2 (5.6). The permutation p-values are 0.018, 0.014 and 0.007, the score bootstrap p-values 0.010, 0.023 and 0.001, and the wild bootstrap p-values on the linear model 0.010, 0.002 and 0.001. In the treated states, hour 0 had 110 road deaths per summer before abolition; after it, observed deaths exceed the counterfactual by 36 per summer in that hour alone, before any offset elsewhere in the day. % reallocation.rds, hours: eve+0 excess_per_season 35.6 (se 9.5).

Panel B reports the morning hour, which turned light. All three estimates are negative: $-3.3$ log points (12.4) for road deaths, $-11.3$ (20.4) for federal highway deaths and $-14.2$ (8.3) for injury crashes. None is significant at the 5 percent level under clustered or permutation inference; the wild bootstrap on the linear model gives $p=0.031$ for federal highway deaths. Light gained in the morning lowered road deaths far less than light lost in the evening raised them, although the two hours had about as many road deaths before abolition (107 and 110 per summer).

Figure~\ref{fig:hours} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) hour by hour around sunset and sunrise. In all three outcomes the estimate peaks at hour 0. For road deaths, the next hour, which went from twilight to night, also rises (16.4 log points, standard error 11.2). Of the other hours, only the second hour before sunrise, dark under both clocks, moves as much (26.4, 13.5). % sunset_design.rds, results: SIM, morning bin -2.
Federal highways show one more feature: crashes in the hour before sunset fall ($-22.3$ log points for injury crashes). Section~\ref{sec:trends} shows that this fall began in 2018/19, the last summer with DST, before abolition.

\subsection{Trends and robustness}\label{sec:trends}

The shaded seasons had no DST.

Figure~\ref{fig:event-study} replaces the single post-abolition indicator with one coefficient per season, shown against the average season with DST, for hour 0 and the hour before it. For road deaths, the coefficients before abolition show no trend (a slope of $-0.5$ log points per season, standard error 2.1) and are jointly indistinguishable from each other ($p=0.18$). % pretrends.rds: pre_trend_lp, pre_trend_se, wald_pre_p.
All five seasons without DST lie above the average season with DST, the first two by the most. For federal highway injury crashes the earlier coefficients drift upward ($p<0.001$ for the joint test). In the hour before sunset, 2018/19 was already low relative to every earlier season, so the fall in that hour predates abolition. % switched_hour_event_study.rds: PRF injury crashes, hour -1, 2008/09-2017/18 between 24.9 and 55.5 log points against 2018/19.

  \label{tab:robustness}

The first and last summers come from one model with a separate effect for 2019/20 and 2020/21 and for 2021/22 to 2023/24. The summer-window row is a difference in differences, treated against control states and after against before, with state and date effects and no off-season. The joint test is a Wald test that the 11 season coefficients before abolition in Figure~\ref{fig:event-study} are equal. Panel B: counterfactual fitted on untreated state-days only, with week and day-of-week effects in place of date effects; 95 percent intervals in brackets, from 299 draws of a state bootstrap. Panel C: in the first row, the control states' events are counted, on each date, in the clock hour that starts at the treated states' standard-time sunset (average over their municipal seats, weighted by road deaths before abolition). The state-by-day row compares hour 0 with hours 3 to 5 before and 2 to 4 after sunset of the same state and day. The two-hour row counts events from standard-time sunset to two hours after it as one bin.   \end{tablenotes}

Table~\ref{tab:robustness} reports checks against these trends and other threats. With a linear treated-by-summer trend fitted on all seasons, the estimate for road deaths is 39.9 log points (20.7). That trend also runs through the seasons after abolition and can absorb part of the effect. Panel B therefore uses a Poisson version of the imputation estimator of \citet{borusyak2024revisiting}, which fits the counterfactual on untreated observations only. With a trend learned before 2019 and extrapolated, road deaths rose 38 percent (95 percent interval $-12$ to 103), against 31 percent (7 to 54) without the trend. Extrapolating the trend costs precision, not effect. On federal highways the trend matters: with it, injury crashes rise by 5.6 log points (8.0) and by 8 percent ($-5$ to 26) in the imputation. We therefore read road deaths for the size of the effect.

In the triple difference (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}, Panel A), the first two seasons without DST give 48.7 log points (11.6) and the last three 15.8 (10.3). The difference does not come from the summer. Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:window-legs} splits the triple difference into its two legs, the gap between treated and control states in the summer window and the same gap in the off-season. In the summer window the gap rose with abolition and stayed up in all five seasons; estimated in the summer window alone, the effect is 39.3 (12.4) in the first two seasons and 31.2 (15.8) in the last three (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). The off-season leg moved instead: it was low in 2019/20, whose off-season includes the pandemic months of April to June 2020, and high in 2021/22 and 2022/23. Dropping every day from March 2020 to February 2022 gives 22.9 (9.1); the summer window alone, which leaves the off-season out, gives 34.5 (13.4) over all five seasons. Across these ways of handling the pandemic and the off-season, the estimate lies between 22.9 and 34.5 log points.

Federal highways also had a shock of their own in the first summer without DST: a presidential order suspended the police's static, mobile and portable speed cameras from mid-August to 23 December 2019 \citep{brasil2019despacho, poder3602019radares}. Without that summer, the federal highway estimates are larger (65.0 for deaths and 25.7 for injury crashes), and the estimate for road deaths, which include deaths on federal highways, is smaller (22.7, standard error 9.8; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}).

The control states kept their clocks, but schedules set on Bras\'ilia time, such as national broadcasts, ran an hour earlier on those clocks every summer with DST and no longer do. Their evening traffic did not move, but their road deaths in hour 0 rose relative to the rest of the day; to the extent that this rise came from those schedules, the triple difference understates the effect. Within the treated states alone, the same comparison of hour 0 with hours of the same day gives 47.2 (7.8) (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:within-group}).

Other comparisons in Panel C of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} leave the estimate in the same range: counting the control states' deaths at the clock time of the treated states' hour 0 on each date, so that both groups are compared at the same time of the evening (33.3, 12.1); state-by-day fixed effects that compare hour 0 with hours of the same state and day whose light did not change (27.7, 12.4); leaving out Carnival and the year-end holidays (30.8, 8.0); and leaving out the 279 oceanfront municipalities, where summer trips to the beach go (36.3, 9.4; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}). Treating the two hours after sunset as one bin lowers the estimate to 21.2 (8.0): the second hour changed less, and adding it dilutes the estimate. No single state or season is decisive: leaving out one state at a time gives between 24.3 and 34.1, and one season at a time between 22.7 and 35.2 (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:leave-out}). The control group matters more: with the eight states of the Northeast alone the estimate is 32.9 (9.2), with the four of the North alone 15.7 (8.8).

The formal sensitivity analysis of \citet{rambachan2023more} adds little here. Its target is the average post-abolition coefficient against 2018/19 alone (14.8 log points), not $\beta$, and with a single reference season that average is too imprecise to rule out small departures from a linear trend (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:honestdid}). % honestdid.rds: avg_post_lp 14.85; breakdown M 0.02.
The case for a causal reading rests on the pattern within the day: the peak in one hour defined by the local sun, the smaller changes in the neighboring hours, the absence of a rise at midday and at night, whose light did not change, and the concentration among pedestrians.

Recorded times heap on the hour and the half hour (34.5 and 23.0 percent of road deaths), so whether a death falls in hour 0 can depend on how its time was rounded. Shifting the hour 0 window by 5 to 15 minutes moves the estimate in the direction light predicts: it is larger when the window starts later and the hour is darker. Spreading each death recorded on the hour or half hour evenly over the 30 minutes around its recorded time gives 31.4 log points (9.5); dropping those deaths altogether leaves 16.7 (12.9), with less than half the sample (Online Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:window-shift}). Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:measurement} collects these checks with those of Section~\ref{sec:data}: the match between death and crash times, the stability of the records across abolition, the extent of heaping, and the estimates with shifted windows or without rounded times.

\subsection{Light, not the clock}\label{sec:dose-results}

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{Darkness as a Dose}
  \label{tab:dose}
  \centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5pt}

The dose of a clock hour is the change abolition brought to its darkness, with a minute of night counted as 1, a minute of civil twilight as one half and a minute of daylight as 0, averaged over the state's municipal seats weighted by their road deaths before abolition. In the morning abolition moved hours from night toward daylight, so the doses there are negative; both panels report the effect of a clock hour going from full daylight to night. Every row has state-by-clock-hour-by-window and state-by-clock-hour-by-season effects. Date effects only: one effect per date, common to all clock hours. Baseline: one effect per clock hour and date. Table~\ref{tab:dose} reports equation~(\ref{eq:dose}). With an effect for every clock hour on every date, an evening clock hour that goes from full daylight to night has 47.7 log points (9.7) more road deaths. With date effects common to all hours instead, the estimate is about the same (45.7, 6.3), so changes after 2019 at particular clock times across the country do not drive it. The last row adds a separate effect for every clock hour in the treated states' summers after abolition, which absorbs any change specific to those states at a given clock time. The dose effect is then identified only by differences in darkness at the same clock hour, which arise because the sun sets at different clock times across the treated states and across the dates of the summer, and it is 52.3 (18.4). For the same change in darkness, the morning coefficient is $-6.4$ (14.7), different from the evening's ($p<0.001$). On federal highways, deaths respond too (79.5, 20.6), and injury crashes less (13.6, 9.0). Pedestrians respond most: a fully dark evening hour raises their road deaths by 115.8 log points (29.7), against 33.6 (11.9) for everyone else. % light_dose.rds, dose: SIM pedestrian and non-pedestrian deaths, spec main.

\subsection{Is it sleep?}

Two features of the design keep acute sleep loss out of the estimates: abolition involved no lost night, and the summer window excludes the weeks after clock changes. A chronic effect through the clock time of sunset \citep{giuntella2019sunset} would run the other way, since an earlier clock sunset should lengthen sleep, not shorten it. And a sleep effect would not confine itself to one hour of the day. Panel D of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) for hours whose light did not change, midday and night. Nothing rises in them: road deaths move by $-4.5$ (5.8) and $-6.6$ (5.6) log points. Federal highway injury crashes fall at night ($-6.1$, $p=0.04$), consistent with the traffic that left the dark evening (Section~\ref{sec:traffic}).

\subsection{Who dies}

\begin{table}[tbp]
  \caption{Pedestrians and Other Road Users in the Hour after Sunset}
  \label{tab:pedestrians}
  \centering\footnotesize
  \input{\tabdir/tab_pedestrians.tex}
  \begin{tablenotes}[Notes]
  Equation~(\ref{eq:main}) for hour 0, estimated separately for events with a pedestrian victim and for all others; Panel C from one stacked model. Inference as in Table~\ref{tab:main}; in each permutation draw both members of the pair receive the same set of treated states, and the difference is divided by the square root of the sum of the two squared standard errors. Excess events are observed minus predicted without abolition, treated states, summer window, after 2019; the pedestrian share of the excess has a delta-method standard error in parentheses.

  \end{tablenotes}
\end{table}

The increase falls disproportionately on pedestrians (Table~\ref{tab:pedestrians}). Pedestrian road deaths in hour 0 rose by 76.6 log points (29.8), more than doubling, while the deaths of all other road users rose by 17.9 (7.8). Pedestrians were 11.7 percent of road deaths in hour 0 before abolition and account for 43.4 percent of the excess after it (standard error 10.3). On federal highways the contrast is sharper: 170 log points for pedestrian deaths against 26 for all others. The pedestrian estimates are significant under the wild bootstrap and the permutation test in all three outcomes. The difference between pedestrians and others is significant on federal highways (permutation $p=0.001$ for deaths and for injury crashes) and borderline for road deaths ($p=0.075$). The federal highway contrast does not come from their trend: with a pre-abolition trend extrapolated, pedestrian deaths there rise by 103.9 log points (34.3) and other deaths by 15.3 (23.5). % mechanism.rds, trend: extrap_lp for PRF pedestrian and non-pedestrian deaths.

Among the other road users (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:road-users}), motorcyclist deaths rose by 19.6 log points (10.9), and the estimate for car occupants is zero but imprecise ($-0.2$, standard error 35.2); deaths in the residual group, 85 percent of them with no type of vehicle recorded, rose by 55.8 (26.4). The ordering among pedestrians, motorcyclists and car occupants is the one visibility predicts. A pedestrian is the road user who most depends on being seen, and pedestrian crash risk is the most sensitive to ambient light around the clock changes \citep{sullivan2002role}; pedestrian deaths at night also fall on brighter moonlit nights \citep{tyndall2025road}. The pattern is also hard to reconcile with sleep, which would impair drivers whoever they hit. The increase was larger on weekends and holidays (41.3, 15.8) than on weekdays (16.1, 10.0), and stays so without Carnival and the year-end holidays (39.3, 16.2), so it is not confined to the commute home. Street lighting points the same way, though imprecisely. When the municipalities of each state are split at the median share of households on unlit streets, the estimate is 42.5 log points (10.0) in the darker half and 10.9 (16.0) in the better-lit half ($p=0.10$ for the difference; Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:lighting}). Among men, about four fifths of the dead, road deaths rose by 33.8 log points (9.9) and federal highway deaths by 65.2 (20.7); for women the estimates are too imprecise to compare (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:sex-age}).

\subsection{Traffic followed the light}\label{sec:traffic}

Drivers adapted to the new light. Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:volume} estimates equation~(\ref{eq:main}) on hourly vehicle counts at federal highway stations. After abolition, traffic in the treated states' summer fell by 6.4 log points (2.2) in hour 0 and by 5.1 (1.3) in the hour before it, and rose by 11.7 (5.0) in the morning hour that turned light, with permutation p-values of 0.069, 0.025 and 0.159. None of the stations counted after abolition had been counted before it: counting resumed in 2021 under a new contract, at new stations (Section~\ref{sec:counts}). On the 30 stations that were moved at most 2 kilometers along the same highway, the evening fall is smaller and not significant ($-3.1$, 3.1) and the morning rise larger (18.7, 5.1).

Subtracting the volume estimate from the crash estimate gives the change in crashes per vehicle. For an equivalent comparison, the crash estimates in that table come from the summers covered by the traffic counts, 2014/15 to 2018/19 and 2021/22 to 2024/25, over which federal highway injury crashes in hour 0 show no trend before abolition ($-2.8$ log points per season, standard error 2.9). % traffic_volume.rds, risk: pre_trend_lp, PRF injury accidents, eve+0.
On those summers, injury crashes in hour 0 rose by 17.6 log points (7.5), and injury crashes per vehicle by 24.0 ($p=0.005$), more than crashes themselves; in the morning hour that turned light, crashes per vehicle fell by 28.1 ($p=0.083$). Fewer vehicles travel in hour 0, and each faces a higher risk. The stations cover federal highways only and say nothing about urban traffic, where many of the pedestrian deaths in the death register occur.

\subsection{The morning does not offset the evening}\label{sec:offset}

  \caption{Excess Events per Summer after Abolition}
  \label{tab:excess}

  \input{\tabdir/tab_excess.tex}

Evening and morning hours may not add to the net because of rounding. Panel B: one model that stacks seven hours (two before to two after standard-time sunset; one before to two after standard-time sunrise) with every fixed effect of equation~(\ref{eq:main}) interacted with the hour; the whole day comes from a separate model. Table~\ref{tab:excess} turns the estimates into events per summer: observed counts in the treated states' summers after abolition minus those predicted without it. Panel A sums every clock hour of the day, weighted by how much its light changed (equation~\ref{eq:dose}). Abolition added 62 road deaths per summer window (standard error 12): 57 in the evening hours that grew darker, and 5 in the morning hours that grew lighter, where the effect is indistinguishable from zero. Extending the estimate to a full DST season under the 2017 rule, about 108 days against the 92 of the window, yields 74 additional deaths (standard error 14). This extension applies coefficients estimated within the summer window to days outside it. The count requires no choice of hours, but it assumes that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected. A dose of zero does not mean that the light did not change at all: the hour before standard-time sunset stayed in daylight, with the sun lower. Panel D of Table~\ref{tab:robustness} finds no detectable change at midday or at night, but with about 580 road deaths a summer in each, its confidence intervals also include a fall as large as the net count. % placebo_hours.rds: 585 and 572 per season; 95 percent intervals about -86 to +42 and -93 to +26 deaths.

Panel B adds up hours estimated one at a time, without that structure. The two evening hours that turned darker added 57 road deaths per summer (standard error 19), and the morning hour that turned light removed 3 (11). That hour gained traffic along with light: on federal highways its vehicles rose by about 12 percent and its injury crashes per vehicle fell by 28 log points (Section~\ref{sec:traffic}), so a lower risk per trip was spread over more trips. Net, these three hours added 54 deaths (20), 17 percent of the deaths predicted in them ($p=0.007$). % reallocation.rds, sums: 54.23, se 20.06, pct_of_cf 17.3, p 0.0069.
Hours $-1$ to $+1$ at each end, from one hour before to two hours after sunset and sunrise, give 53 (35), and all seven hours 41 (41). Estimated directly, the whole day gives $-5$ deaths (66). That estimate adds the variation of every hour of the day to an effect concentrated in a few, so its standard error exceeds the evening effect. The whole-day count can therefore neither confirm the net figure nor rule it out, and we do not read it as evidence that abolition only moved deaths between hours of the day. On federal highways, the dose model gives 31 deaths (12) per summer; injury crashes, whose response to darkness is weaker, net 43 (57).

In levels, a clock hour that goes from full daylight to night has about 61 percent more road deaths, and more than three times as many pedestrian deaths. That pedestrians bear so much of the increase matches evidence that their crash risk in the dark is up to seven times that in daylight \citep{sullivan2002role}. The effect on all road users is larger than projections for the United States. Over the three hours of Panel B, abolition added 17 percent to the predicted road deaths, while \citet{coate2004effects} project that year-round DST would lower deaths in the morning and evening periods it affects by 13 percent for pedestrians and 3 percent for vehicle occupants. Part of the gap may be who is on the road: before abolition, pedestrians and motorcyclists were 35 percent of road deaths in hour 0 of the treated states' summer, and motorcyclist deaths rose with abolition, by less than pedestrian deaths and by more than those of car occupants. % road_users.rds: pre_per_season pedestrian 12.8 + motorcyclist 25.5 of 109.9.

\subsection{Before and after travel adjusted}\label{sec:transitions}

Abolition measures the effect of a darker evening after five summers in which people could change when they travel. The clock changes before 2019 measure the same change of light before travel had time to adjust. When the clocks went back each February, the evening hour 0 went from daylight to dark overnight, while work, school and travel kept to the same clock hours; when they went forward each spring, the reverse. Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:transitions} compares hour 0 in the three weeks after each change with the three weeks before, in the treated against the control states, and uses the same calendar days of the seasons after abolition, when no clock moved, to net out the seasonal change. In the three weeks after the clocks went back, road deaths in hour 0 rose by 54.6 log points (21.9); after they went forward, deaths fell by 29.9 (18.5). Read as the effect of a darker evening, the two average 42.3 (13.8), against 29.2 after abolition. Each change also adds or removes an hour of sleep, which acts on every hour of the day and pushes both transition estimates toward zero; compared with hours of the same day, which nets it out, the transitions give 79.1 (14.2), against 27.7 (12.4) for abolition. In one model that allows for the overlap of the two samples, abolition minus the clock changes is $-13.1$ (12.5) in the first comparison and $-51.4$ (18.3) in the second. Only the second, which nets out sleep, separates them. The two settings also differ in the time of year, and the effect of abolition is not the same across the summer window (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window-parts}). From 15 November to 7 December, while schools are in session, abolition raised road deaths in hour 0 by 58.1 log points (12.6). From 24 December to 15 January it is $-12.3$ (16.8). From 16 to 31 January it is 49.1 (15.6), although schools are still on break then in every treated state but Goi\'as \citep{saopaulo2018resolucao, goias2018parecer, minas2023ano}. The school calendar alone therefore cannot explain how the estimate varies across the summer window: no increase is detectable from Christmas to mid-January, while the late-January school break shows about as large an effect as the school weeks. The three weeks after each clock change fall while schools are in session, the same part of the school year as the weeks from mid-November to early December. Compared with abolition in those weeks, the clock changes are not distinguishable from it: the difference is 15.8 (18.0) in hour 0 and $-22.2$ (20.9) against hours of the same day (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:transitions}). The gap over the whole window thus points mainly to the weeks from Christmas to mid-January rather than to a uniformly smaller effect after travel adjusted. In the school weeks, the effect of a darker evening after five summers is close to its effect in the weeks after a clock change, though the intervals leave room for a moderate decline. Late January gives an estimate of about the same size. The gap between those weeks and the school weeks changes little without the oceanfront municipalities or without Par\'a, a control state whose 2019 school year ran from March 2019 to January 2020 \citep{para2018calendario}, and before abolition the parts of the window moved alike (Online Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window-parts}). These checks do not rule out holiday travel as an explanation, and the data do not say why no increase is detectable in those weeks. On federal highways the same comparison gives 121 log points for deaths at the clock changes against 54 after abolition, and about the same for injury crashes (20.6 against 22.2).

Table~\ref{tab:cost} scales and values the net count of the dose model. Column 1 reports the estimated increase in road deaths with a recorded time: 62 deaths per summer window and 74 when extended to the full DST season (Table~\ref{tab:excess}). Both counts assume, as discussed in Section~\ref{sec:offset}, that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected. The full season is the relevant unit for the policy comparison, since reinstating DST would restore all of it. The 74 deaths apply the average effect of the summer window to the extra days, in early November and mid-February; that average includes the weeks from Christmas to mid-January, when no increase was detectable (Section~\ref{sec:transitions}). Refitting the dose model with a separate effect for each part of the window and applying the effect of 15 November to 7 December to the extra days yields 79 deaths (Table~\ref{tab:excess}). Early November falls in the same part of the school year as 15 November to 7 December; mid-February, when many school systems are reopening, may be closer to the smaller estimate for 1 to 14 February. Because the extra days lie outside the estimation window, 79 is a sensitivity calculation. % light_dose.rds, dose: season_net_term 78.8 (SIM, main).
 The summer-window deaths are 1.0 percent of all land-transport deaths in the treated states' summer window. Column 2 assumes that road deaths without a recorded time fall in the affected hours in the same proportion as those with one, which gives 77 per summer window. Column 3 also assumes that deaths off the road, 85 percent of them in hospitals, follow deaths on the road in proportion, which gives 157; it is an extrapolation, because the design cannot place an in-hospital death in the hour of its crash, and the direction of its error is unknown: a pedestrian struck in the dark may be more or less likely than other victims to die at the scene.

We value a death with the reference rule of \citet{robinson2019valuing} for transferring a value of a statistical life (VSL) to a lower-income country: the US ratio of VSL to income per head, 160, extrapolated to Brazil with an income elasticity of 1.5, so that $\mathit{VSL}_{\mathit{BR}} = 160\, Y_{\mathit{US}}\, (Y_{\mathit{BR}}/Y_{\mathit{US}})^{1.5}$, where $Y$ is gross national income per head at purchasing power parity in 2025 \citep{worldbank2026wdi}. The resulting VSL is 1.8 million international dollars, or R\$4.7 million at the 2025 parity rate (Online Appendix~\ref{app:cost} gives the inputs and the alternative rules). We report every value in 2025 international dollars, a unit with the purchasing power that a US dollar has in the United States; reais are converted at the purchasing-power-parity rate, not at the exchange rate. % total_cost.rds, vsl: 1,825,618 international dollars; R$ 4.66338 million.
At that value, the deaths in one summer window have an estimated cost of 114 million international dollars (standard error 22), rising to 287 million under the broadest scaling; over a whole season of DST, the deaths in column 1 cost 135 million. The two alternative rules of \citet{robinson2019valuing} give larger values, up to 571 million per summer window. A human-capital valuation of a death on a federal highway \citep{ipea2015acidentes}, which leaves out the value of life itself, gives 19 to 49 million. % total_cost.rds, value: DST season, count A, rule (a): 134.7 (se 26.3). Two costs are not valued. Nonfatal injuries rose too, as the federal highway injury crashes show, but the death register has no counterpart for them, and the federal highway series is sensitive to its trend. Nor does the count include what the people who moved their travel out of the dark hour gave up to do so; the deaths are the harm that remained after that avoidance.

The energy side of the ledger has changed sign over time. The technical note behind the 2019 decision estimated that DST had raised electricity load by about 0.7 percent \citep{mme2019nota}; on that estimate, abolition saved a little electricity at the price of the deaths in the darkened evenings. For today's system, the grid operator estimates that reinstating DST would save 96 to 139 million international dollars in thermal-generation fuel in one summer and, by lowering the evening peak by about 2 GW, about 0.7 billion a year in payments for reserve capacity \citep{ons2024nota}. % ONS reais (R$244-356 million; R$1.8 billion) converted at the 2025 PPP factor, 2.55441. These figures come from a different method and are not strictly comparable with the ones here. Taken at face value, they make the two sides of the ledger point the same way: reinstating DST would save fuel worth about as much as the reference value of the deaths of a season in column 1, and capacity payments that, if realized, are larger. Neither side counts the two clock changes a year that abolition removed, whose cost the literature attributes to lost sleep in the days after the spring change: more road crashes \citep{smith2016spring, gillmore2025daylight} and, in Brazil, more deaths from heart attacks \citep{toro2015daylight}. The summer window excludes those weeks, so this paper does not measure that cost.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

When Brazil stopped moving its clocks, the evening hour that lost its sunlight became deadlier on the road, disproportionately for pedestrians, and the morning hour that gained light did not compensate. The deaths followed the local sun, not the clock. Counting only deaths at the scene with a recorded time, and assuming that hours that remained in full daylight or full darkness were unaffected, abolition of DST added 62 road deaths from mid-November to mid-February each year, and about 74 if the effect is extended to the rest of the season. In the weeks when schools were in session, the effect of abolition over the five summers without DST was close to the effect at the clock changes, when the light moved overnight and travel had no time to adjust; across the summer, the increase was not detectable from Christmas to mid-January but was detectable in late January, when most treated states were still on school break.

The estimates have limits that matter for their use. They count only deaths at the scene with a recorded time, not deaths off the road or without a recorded time, nor nonfatal injuries. Their sample has 23 states and five summers without DST, two of them in the pandemic; the estimate lies between 23 and 34 log points across the ways of handling the pandemic and the off-season, and in the summer comparison it shows no clear decline over the five seasons. The net count over the day assumes that hours with no change in the modeled darkness dose were unaffected; estimated without that restriction, the whole-day effect is too imprecise to say whether some deaths moved to other hours. Federal highway records are sensitive to a pre-existing trend, and the traffic counts cover only federal highways.

For Brazil, the estimates answer the policy question directly: the choice between reinstating seasonal DST and maintaining year-round standard time is the comparison this paper measures, and Section~\ref{sec:cost} puts the lives on the same ledger as the energy. Elsewhere the numbers travel less far. In summer, seasonal and permanent DST set the same clock, so the estimates are the cost, in summer evenings, of choosing permanent standard time over either. They say nothing about winter, when permanent DST would darken the mornings, and they are least informative at latitudes higher than Brazil's. Nor do they weigh the clock changes, energy use or the effects of the clock on sleep. Part of what people did to protect themselves, driving less in the hour that turned dark, is already in the estimates. Within these limits, darker evenings cost lives on the road that brighter mornings do not return, and a disproportionate share of those lives are pedestrians, whom street lighting and road design can protect when the clock does not.
